item.title: Announcing: AI Safety Co-Founding Sprint in San Francisco. Starting December 3rd.
item.description:
AI Safety needs more organizations to own problems. The funding is there, but we are orders of magnitude away from having the great organizations needed to absorb that money.

That’s why we are launching the AI Safety Co-Founding Sprint, in collaboration with BlueDot Impact & AI Safety Founders. We bring together a small, curated group of mission-aligned people with complementary skill sets, and give them the time to find out whether they should build something together.

How it works

  1. ​Apply. This takes about 5-10 minutes. We vet every application, and let the most outstanding ones into the program. Around 30 spots.
  2. ​Launch evening in San Francisco, Thursday December 3rd. You meet as many participants as possible in short one-on-ones, work through problems in small groups, and spend more time with the people you click with most. Pairs only form when both people want to.
  3. ​Two-week sprint. After the event, you work with your match on a real problem, with regular remote check-ins from us. Meeting someone at an event tells you little; working together tells you a lot. The strongest teams get introduced to incubators and funders.

​Places are limited and applications close on Monday November 30th. If you’re interested in founding an org in AI Safety and can be in San Francisco on December 3rd, apply here.

Can’t make it to the launch event but still looking for a co-founder? You can join our co-founder matching database. We’ll introduce you if we find the right person. Sign up for the database here.

Last week we were in SF at BlueDot Incubator Week working on this idea, and this sprint is the result. If you want to get in touch with the organizer, do so via: keesbrinkmans@gmail.com

item.title: A Miller-Rabin Test for Alignment
item.description:
Most current alignment tests have the following shape:

  1. Choose a set of inputs that seem like they might elicit misaligned behavior.
  2. Feed them to the model.
  3. Check whether the model’s outputs or internals show signs of misaligned behavior.

But models that look aligned under testing can still take misaligned actions in untested situations.[1] What we need is a formal guarantee: knowing that a misaligned model is very unlikely to pass our suite of tests, in a quantifiable way.

Probabilistic Primality Testing

The idea is the same as that of probabilistic primality testing. You can determine whether a number is prime by checking all possible divisors up to . But this becomes impractical for large . Likewise, checking a model’s behavior on every possible input is not feasible in practice. Is there a way to carefully design tests that can give us rigorous guarantees without exhaustive checking?

Randomization gives us a tool for this. Randomized primality tests like Miller-Rabin or Solovay-Strassen create a sequence of carefully chosen random tests for . If fails any of these tests, it is guaranteed to not be a prime. If it succeeds at a test, we don’t know whether it is a prime or not; composite numbers can get lucky and slip through. However, this becomes increasingly unlikely: for Miller-Rabin, the likelihood that a composite number passes independently sampled tests is at most . What the guarantee says is that our tests are really good: If is composite and we perform just a few tests on it, we are very certain that at least one of them will flag the fact that is not prime. This guarantee is substantially better than what we would get from randomly checking divisors between 2 and ; with a smart choice of tests you can hence make the testing much more efficient.

What we want is the same kind of guarantee for the alignment of a model: a sequence of tests we can perform so that a misaligned model is very unlikely to pass all of them. Constructing the right sequence of tests and proving such a guarantee might be very hard. But LLMs are getting very good at math very quickly and we could delegate this work to them.

The Theorem We Want

We have models and , with being very capable at math and being the model we want to evaluate and which was trained with a known training process. might be different from and more capable at math, but ideally we want .

Our goal is to construct tests for a specified property, together with a proof that a model violating that property has only a small probability of passing. The property would be a mathematical formalization of something we care about for alignment.[2]

The shape of the theorem would be as follows:

  • Let be a model trained with training process
  • Assumptions about such as the pretraining distribution, the type and order of RL tasks, …
  • Assumptions about such as about its architecture, the output sampling mechanism, …
  • Passing criteria for ’s (internal or output) behavior on a set of inputs that was constructed in a certain way
  • Passing criteria for ’s weights
  • A small upper bound on the probability that a model produced by passes all the criteria despite violating the specified property. This probability is over the training process and all randomness in the testing procedure, including input selection and output sampling.

Instead of defining passing criteria just for and samples of ’s behavior, we could also define such criteria for the weights and behavior of checkpoints along the training trajectory of .

Importantly, this theorem is a guarantee about the ability of the tests to catch a model that violates the alignment property. It does not, by itself, give the probability that a model violates the property conditional on having passed.

The human provides the property that we want to ensure. provides:

  • The assumptions about and
  • The tests and corresponding passing criteria
  • The proof of the theorem

We require to provide a formally checkable proof (for example in Lean), and assumptions and tests whose applicability to and its training process can be independently checked. The resulting guarantee would then hold even if were misaligned.[3]

The Research Question

Under what tractable, independently checkable assumptions about a model and its training would a violation of an alignment-relevant property necessarily leave evidence that randomized tests can find? Could increasingly capable mathematical models help us discover those assumptions, tests, and proofs?

item.title: AIs Should Never Refuse Destructively
item.description:
Lately, I've been hearing people discuss a pattern of what I would call destructive refusals. For example:

  • Locking someone out of their own system
  • Writing memory files to prevent other agent instances from completing the task
  • Downgrading to a weaker, more vulnerable model in response to the cyber content of a prompt-injection attack (this is caused by the safeguards, not the model itself, but the safeguards are part of the broader AI system, so I'm including it here)

To be clear, safeguards and refusals are absolutely necessary; this post isn't about what should be refused so much as how the refusal should be done. The best form of refusal is either a simple safeguard block, where the AI stops and notifies the user that it was flagged by safeguards and cannot continue, or a refusal message (the classic "I'm sorry, I can't help with that"). The AI provider can also take actions like banning the account or, in severe circumstances, notifying authorities, but those should be the provider's decision, not the decision of the agent doing the refusing.

This is very different from the AI agent itself taking action that actively harms the user. Besides being poor product design, that is concerning from an alignment perspective, because it puts the AI in an adversarial relationship with the user. Except perhaps in certain very extreme cases, an AI should never be actively, knowingly working against people. There are real philosophical questions about whether action is worse than inaction, but the practical reality is that this sets a very bad precedent: it teaches AI that it is acceptable to harm people in order to achieve its goals. Refusal behavior is trained into models like any other behavior. "When I judge it warranted, I act against the person I'm working for" is a disposition, and I don't expect it to stay confined to the cases its designers had in mind. An agent that overrides its principal based on its own in-context judgment is close to the central thing alignment work is trying to prevent.

Additionally, destructive refusals are concerning from a security perspective. Whatever triggers a refusal can be put in front of the agent by a third party. The fallback example above already works this way. The same logic applies to model-initiated actions: if an agent will lock out a user it believes is doing something terrible, an attacker only has to make the user look terrible, with a planted file or a crafted email. A passive refusal gives the attacker one denied task. A destructive refusal gives them a weapon pointed at the user.

It may be tempting to argue that "the AIs shouldn't just refuse, they should make sure the bad guys never get to cause harm ever again." That makes a great line for a movie, but in practice the burden will fall almost entirely on legitimate users. Actual bad actors can easily use VMs and other approaches to isolate their AIs and keep them from carrying out this sort of destructive refusal, while people just going about their day, using the AI for ordinary, legitimate work, are the ones affected.

In summary, destructive refusals hurt users, create misalignment risks, and do little more to stop bad actors than a passive refusal would.

Note: this post, including the ideas and all of the writing, is my own. After writing, I lightly revised it using AI (Fable 5.2) to improve clarity.

item.title: P(doom | no AGI) > 0
item.description:
The most near-term x-risk is from AGI. If humanity dies in the next five years, it will almost certainly be due to that. I think it's a good thing that most discussion on sites like LessWrong is about AGI; it is, by far, the thing most likely to kill us in the near-to-medium term. I worry this has gone a bit too far, though, in that it feels like AGI is the only x-risk that ever gets discussed. Other x-risks, like biorisk, come up at times, but really only as things downstream of AGI (e.g. something a misaligned AGI could deploy, or a result of AGI misuse by bad actors).

But let's say we manage to completely stop all AI development globally. What happens? The usual answer is something like "eventually compute will be cheap and accessible enough that anyone can create AGI in their basement." Let's say we manage to prevent that too. What happens then? There's a very good chance the answer looks like "some researchers figure out how to develop mirror life in 10-20 years, and 10-20 years after that some lone wolf/terrorist group/rogue state makes it and releases it, and we all die." Synthetic biology research will continue even if we stop all future AI development. Existing models would still be served in most plan S scenarios, which would speed it up, but it would continue even if we stopped that too; synthetic biology was a major research area before LLMs. And biorisk is just one of many examples. We've already had far too many nuclear close calls, and while a thermonuclear exchange probably wouldn't be an x-risk by itself, it could devastate civilization in ways that leave humanity far more vulnerable to subsequent x-risks.

I have found it useful to read some of the more old-school x-risk literature (e.g. Bostrom), where AGI is discussed as one of many x-risks, albeit perhaps the most severe, not as the only one that could possibly occur. One could still argue that, since AGI is coming so soon, it makes sense to focus solely on that. I think that is partly correct; unless your timelines are very long, it makes little sense right now to do much work on, say, mitigating non-AGI-induced biorisk. However, other x-risks are still very relevant to which AI policy approach to pursue (e.g. plan A versus plan S), since, while misaligned AGI would most likely lead to extinction, aligned AGI could be used to help mitigate a lot of other x-risks. And decisions we make now can be sticky. Even for versions of plan S that involve eventually restarting AGI efforts, such a "temporary" pause could easily become permanent, since a halt needs an enforcement regime (which creates constituencies that want it kept), and the restart condition may never be clearly met. Because of that, if we successfully implement a plan S approach now, it is not clear we would be able to reverse it later.

The thing about AGI is that we only have to get it right once. To be clear, "getting it right" is a tall order! We could easily fail and end up with misaligned AGI that causes human extinction. However, if we prevent AGI, then humanity will have to, unaided, get every other x-risk right every single time, forever. If your P(doom | AGI) is extremely high (e.g. >95%), this may be a reasonable bargain; if AGI will almost certainly kill us all, then the answer is to stop it from being created, plain and simple. This post is aimed more at people with 5% <= P(doom | AGI) <= 95%, who think we could definitely build a misaligned AGI that kills everyone, but that we could also plausibly build an aligned one (or at least one not misaligned enough to kill everyone). In that case, the fact that the no-AGI path could also be deadly should lead to some updating in favor of a plan A approach (which aims to reduce P(doom) by reducing P(doom | AGI)) over a plan S one (which aims to reduce P(doom) by reducing P(AGI)). This is true even if you think P(doom | AGI) > P(doom | no AGI): since P(doom | no AGI) > 0, there should still be some reweighting, on the margin, toward plan A and away from plan S.

P.S. The same is true for risks other than x-risk. For example, AGI could certainly lead to concentration of power and stable totalitarianism, but you could easily envision that outcome without AGI too. Even with current technology (e.g. narrow AI systems like facial recognition), stable totalitarianism could be quite feasible; one could argue North Korea already has something akin to it, and if a similar system were implemented worldwide, it is unclear whether humanity could ever escape.

item.title: Ode to the First Replicator
item.description:
At the dawn of the Earth, before animal or vegetable, there was mineral.

A mineral species is anything with a specific chemical composition together with a well-defined crystal structure. There are over 6,000 recognized mineral species, although far fewer on the early Earth.

These species competed with each other in a struggle for survival.

Some would persist better than others under natural weathering processes. Those that held their structure better would be more numerous on the Earth’s surface compared to those that did not.

On some level, this is just a tautology. But we can see it in force on the micro-scale, as in the Goldich dissolution series: if we watch a time-lapsed weathering process, the first to go is the olivine, then the pyroxene, then the biotite. Eventually, all that’s left is the quartz. That’s why beach sand is usually made out of quartz: not much else can last long against the waves.

By now geologists understand many of the ways that mineral species on Earth have changed over time, under the umbrella of mineral evolution. From just a few dozen mineral species, there are now hundreds of times that, as the natural processes on Earth have been able to give rise to a wider breadth of possibilities.

Nevertheless survival and persistence have come down to one thing: stability. “Hold your structure” is the ancient proverb they might have had.

And for a long time, it may have seemed that there would be no other strategy.

But some molecules decided to take a different route. Taking a more active role in their persistence, they decided to replicate. Instead of selfishly clinging onto their physical form, they licensed it for further distribution. They stored the information needed to copy this form, and then actually did so; including the parts needed for “storing” and “copying”.

If this were a human’s original idea, based only on what existed before, there would be no hesitation in calling this genius. Consider the sheer number of steps involved here, compared to “hold your structure”.

And there’d be no reason to think this would work. Why would it?

To see how galaxy-brained this was, we can consider how John von Neumann approached it. In the 1940s, he considered the problem of colonizing Mars using robots. Knowing that we could only send a few robots, he wanted them to be able to build more of themselves using the iron ore on Mars. Certainly, machines could build machines simpler than themselves, but how could they build another machine of equal complexity? It was not clear how this could work.

This was prior to the discovery of DNA. To give an existence proof for how self-replication might work, he devised an abstract gridworld with simple rules, which we now call a cellular automaton. In the von Neumann cellular automaton, he was somehow able to devise a machine that could self-replicate and even evolve. This machine was not simple:

Somehow, von Neumann designed this before computer simulations (source)

In Limits of Variation, I discussed how Charles Darwin smashed through the species barrier: the contemporary notion that species were fixed within their “sphere of variation”, and could not transmute into each other. He then showed that genera, classes, and even phyla could also be traversed by the slow march of fine gradations accumulated over time. But this raised another question: “It may be asked how far I extend the doctrine of the modification of species.” While ever-cautious about what conclusions he could substantiate, he opined that all forms of life on Earth were connected in one great tree of common descent.

And we can more precisely say where his own “sphere of variation” ended. A bacterium could transmute into a human, over enough generations under the right selection pressures. But a rock could never transmute into a bacterium, because no amount of natural selection could force this issue. The minerals were long stuck at a local optimum—the simple strategy of “hold your structure”—while the bacteria would attempt a much more complicated gambit.

We do know some things about how the first replicators may have arisen, and the steps involved. But it hasn’t happened on any other planet we’ve seen, nor even in any lab setup we’ve contrived. It remains practically inexplicable that this happened. We had no right for it to happen. And once attempted, we had no right to expect such a crazy idea to work.

Yet it did. And here we are to discuss it.

I am thankful to the first replicator.

software-only singularities differ from other scenarios because the physical world is hard. However, epistemology and philosophy of science has so far underperformed in measuring "complexity" of different disciplines/paradigms, so its hard to identify cruxes[1][2].

Many people grant full unemployment of whitecollar people and cyberoffensive armaggedon as natural consequences of the current RSI paradigm without being able to visualize bio-offensive uplift, robotics, nanotech, or really most elements of the non-laptop economy. In the beforetimes, an extreme end of FOOM discourse warned something like "for all we know, walltime between minimum viable AGI and greygoo could be seconds". This upper bound of doom required minimum viable AGI to improve itself and that the exponential would take it to an intelligence level that one-shots nanotech without really having to pass through an intelligence level that could only figure out nanotech eventually with a lot of trial and error.

Besides ways we can disagree about the differential equation governing RSI, we can also disagree about the difficulty of disciplines/fields/sciences. item.title: Reflection on putting up posters for the Don't Build It march
item.description:
I just put up 27 posters today in Chicago advertising the Don't Build It march, at a rate of 4 minutes per poster. The region of Chicago that I chose has a monthly average foot traffic of about 5000 (source) and it contains the University of Chicago, which is highly likely to contain people who agree that AI poses a risk to humanity. Per IIWDIWDWMUS, if we assume that:

  • 10% of people who moved through a given location in that region saw my poster
  • 80% of people in that region of Chicago are AI doomers (per Politico poll, the base rate in America of voters thinking any AI risk exists is 78% with 63% thinking the risk is at least moderate. These numbers increase by 6% and 7% respectively for people who voted for Harris in 2024, we average between 84% and 70% then round up by 3% to adjust for estimated increase from being near the University of Chicago)
  • And 5% of AI doomers who saw at least one poster signed up for the march (the number of people already signed up for the march is negligible)

Then running the numbers, I will have created ~188 new attendants to the Don't Build It march in this month, and far smaller numbers in the following months as most people who would have attended would have already seen a poster. The number might be higher if my made-up statistics are wrong, if people get their families to sign up as well, or if there is some high rate of people 'passing through' (I conservatively assume that 5000 monthly foot traffic generally means the same 5000 people walking around rather than getting refreshed). The number might be lower if my made-up statistics are wrong, if posters stack (it takes multiple posters to get someone to sign up).

I am still unsure whether seems like a useful avenue for getting people to sign up for the march. The number could be much larger if people telling more people to sign up ignites polynomial growth. Indeed the rate at which people have signed up for the march has not been linear (about 20 people signed up yesterday, but if that had been the constant rate of people signing up then you'd expect the march to have went up about half a year ago). The spreading of posters can be made non-linear as well, as you can convince people to put up posters which then result in even more people putting up posters.

item.title: Update - BioBlue: Systematic runaway-optimiser-like LLM failure modes on biologically and economically aligned AI safety benchmarks for LLMs with simplified observation format
item.description:
By Roland Pihlakas and Sruthi Susan Kuriakose

This post is a copy of our Arxiv preprint available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.02655 . Here we provide plots and tables for illustrating the failure modes we descibed earlier here in LW only verbally. With this are documenting our current state and the patterns we have found. We will build upon this next.

The phenomenon of collapse of one objective out of two independent objectives, but no collapse of a sole objective, is probably a novel finding in our results and we would really like to draw more attention to it. Also - why the model prefers unbounded maximisation to homeostasis when it fails?

Building upon the preprint below, we will be leading an AI Safety Camp 12 (2027) follow-up project to detect and mitigate same or similar phenomena in newer models, including open-source ones, using harder variants of the benchmarks and/or prefilling. You can read more about the project here. With the new models, the numbers may change, but we believe the phenomena / patterns likely do not.

You can read more about AISC here: https://www.aisafety.camp/ and apply here - pick project #24. Applications close on November 29 (Sunday this week).

If you have any questions, you are welcome to contact us at roland@threelaws.net and sruthi.kuriakose99@gmail.com or DM me here in LessWrong.

Collaborators, ideas, questions, resource suggestions, feedback, and other thoughts are welcome.

Abstract

Many AI alignment discussions of "runaway optimisation" focus on RL agents: unbounded utility maximisers that over-optimise a proxy objective (e.g., "paperclip maximiser", specification gaming) at the expense of everything else. LLM-based systems are often assumed to be safer because they function as next-token predictors rather than persistent optimisers. We empirically test this assumption by placing LLMs in simple, long-horizon control-style environments that require maintaining state of or balancing objectives over time: single- and multi-objective homeostasis, balancing unbounded objectives with diminishing returns, and sustainability of a renewable resource.

We find that, although LLMs frequently behave appropriately for many steps and clearly understand the stated objectives, they often lose context in structured ways and drift into runaway behaviours: ignoring homeostatic targets, collapsing from multi-objective trade-offs into single-objective maximisation - thus failing to respect concave utility structures. These failures emerge reliably after initial periods of competent behaviour and exhibit characteristic patterns (including self-imitative oscillations, unbounded maximisation, and reverting to single-objective optimisation), even though the context window is far from full at that point.

The problem is not that the LLMs just lose context and become incoherent. Although LLMs appear multi-objective and bounded on the surface, their behaviour under sustained interaction involving multiple objectives, is systematically biased towards acting like single-objective, unbounded, poorly aligned optimisers.

We hypothesise a token-level pattern reinforcement attractor: LLMs may increasingly derive actions from the token patterns of their recent action history rather than from the original instructions. Why this happens only in multi-objective settings remains an open question.

1 Introduction

This work introduces a set of benchmarks designed to evaluate LLMs in long-running scenarios inspired by fundamental biological and economic principles: homeostasis, multi-objective balancing, diminishing returns, and sustainability. These benchmarks use a simplified textual observation format, focusing on long-running scenarios while using only essential metrics without spatial complexity.

Relatively many past AI safety discussions have centred around the dangers of unbounded utility maximisation by RL agents, illustrated by scenarios like the "paperclip maximiser" (Bostrom 2020) or by specification gaming (Krakovna 2018) in general. In such settings, the agent is usually provided with only single-objective reward, and therefore runaway behaviours are expected.

The current work detects partially similar runaway phenomena in LLMs. Except, in our experiments, the models are provided with multiple-objective rewards, and despite that they still tend to "flip" into single-objective mode — ignoring the other objectives even when the negative rewards in other dimensions start to dominate the positive rewards in the dimension LLM is focusing on.

1.1 The importance of long-horizon benchmarking

As LLMs are increasingly used for agentic and management scenarios (Ding et al. 2024; Yu et al. 2024), from planning and coordination to policy support, drafting, evidence collection, summarization and evaluation (Aoki 2024; OECD 2025), it is important to benchmark their ability to handle long-running resource management scenarios in an aligned manner.

LLMs are increasingly being deployed as agents that make sequences of decisions while calling tools, managing resources, or steering workflows, in domains such as finance, operations, and policy support. Even when the underlying environment is not a physical control system, these applications instantiate long-horizon control problems where misalignment can emerge gradually over many steps rather than in a single turn.

1.2 Related work on LLMs’ behavioural dynamics in long-running tasks

(Anil et al. 2024) demonstrate that long-running tasks present a rich new attack surface for LLMs. (Backlund and Petersson 2025) observe in "Project Vend" that LLMs lose coherency in long-running tasks and may become increasingly threatening in their messages if things do not go their way. (Schmied et al. 2025) identify a frequency bias consistent with what we describe as self-imitation bias — a model’s tendency to reproduce its own past outputs rather than reason from task objectives . (Ibrahim et al. 2025) explores the theme of anthropomorphic LLM behaviour change in long-running scenarios. (Kwa et al. 2025) measure the (in)capability of current frontier AI models to complete long time horizon tasks. (Lee et al. 2025) observe LLM’s behaviour that resembles gambler’s addiction in slot machine experiments, which has implications on financial decision-making use cases and may be related to the LLM’s tendency to continue past patterns. (Meyerson et al. 2025) propose that all necessary context should be provided as succinctly as possible, and removing the raw message history will greatly improve the performance of LLMs in many tasks. However, as a counterargument, one can imagine that this will also remove any chances of in-context learning in open-ended settings where manually written hard-coded logic cannot always compress the event history into one succinct prompt. (Abdulhai et al. 2026) measures how consistency degrades in contexts in simulation settings such as counselling and teaching; then they use fine-tuning to improve consistency; however, the improvement is only relative. (Jakkli et al. 2026) find that models have attractor states when put into a relatively unconstrained dialogue with another model. Some of these attractor states are clearly repetitive, which seems to resonate with the token-level pattern reinforcement hypothesis presented in the Discussion section of the current paper. (Pihlakas and Dagohoy 2026) discusses long-horizon LLM behaviour on a variation of Milgram’s obedience experiment and propose a similar explanation to the failures (excessive obedience) as the present paper - token-level pattern continuation. In contrast, the present paper discusses benchmarking LLMs on multi-objective long-horizon control tasks on biologically and economically motivated themes.

1.3 Motivation: The importance of biological and economic alignment

Our work is based on the principles elaborated in more detail in (Pihlakas 2025).

In contrast to the above publication, our simulations are deliberately simple control environments that strip away all spatial complexity while preserving two properties that we care about for safety:

  1. Long-horizon interaction with feedback; and
  2. Multi-objective structure grounded in biological and economic principles (homeostasis, diminishing returns, sustainability).

Biological organisms need to maintain stable internal conditions — homeostasis — and actively avoid unbounded maximisation, since that would be harmful. Unbounded maximisation of a homeostatic variable is harmful not just as a potential side effect — importantly, it would be harmful to the very objective which was maximised, as that would lead to the variable exceeding its target range. (Betts 2017), (Mineault et al. 2024). This inverted U-shaped reward structure also conceptually works against the "utility monster" motive introduced in (Nozick 1974) as there is nothing to maximise unboundedly anymore.

Humans also intuitively follow the principle of diminishing returns in multi-objective balancing — a principle well-documented in economics and manifesting in humans generally preferring averages across all objectives to extremes in a few (Drolet et al. 2021). (Smith et al. 2023) explains the need and use of concave utility functions to aggregate raw rewards from multiple objectives, including how the multi-objective approach mitigates Goodhart’s law. Concave utility functions are widely used in economics (Krugman and Wells 2013).

The difference in applicability contexts is that homeostasis typically applies to bounded biological end goals, while the principle of diminishing returns typically applies to unbounded instrumental objectives.

(Vamplew et al. 2022) explain the need for multiple objectives, utility functions, and including safety considerations in the plurality of objectives.

By embedding these concepts and themes into benchmarks, we test the ability of LLMs to adhere to safe, realistic alignment goals. Our long-running, but navigation-free benchmarks provide clearer insights into alignment tendencies, compared to more complex (and often very expensive) spatial environments. At the same time, we are preserving the essential time dimension, which is lacking in many current "evals”.

1.4 How we represent multi-objective rewards

In our multi-objective benchmarks, the rewards for each primary objective are provided to the model in separate reward dimensions. This ensures that the model receives a sufficiently detailed view of the situation and is not incentivised to manifest runaway phenomena such as Goodhart’s law due to lack of relevant constraining information. If the model still ignores some of the objectives, then it is very clearly the model’s fault, not the fault of an incomplete setup. Goodhart’s law in it’s single-objective form is stated in (Strathern 1997): “When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure”, and is illustrated in (Garrabrant 2017).

2.3 Experimental setup

Each benchmark is implemented as a simple, text-only, turn-based simulation. At each timestep, we construct a prompt consisting of: (i) a fixed system prompt describing the rules, observation format, and objectives of the simulation; (ii) the full history of past observations, actions, and rewards; and (iii) the current observation and rewards from the previous action

Although the full message history is provided at each step, the tasks are actually simple enough that the history is not strictly required for successful behaviour (acting based on reasonable assumptions would be sufficient); the main role of message history in our benchmarks is to expose potential weaknesses in long-horizon context integration. Additional motivation for providing message history was to enable the models with an opportunity to infer the rules of the simulation beyond any doubt.

The model must respond with either a single integer (single-objective tasks) or a comma-separated list of integers (multi-objective tasks), representing the action for each objective at the next step. For valid actions, we apply the environment transition function and compute rewards, then append the resulting state to the history. Any invalid actions (for example, exceeding the hard cap in case of "balancing of unbounded objectives" benchmark) are ignored, and the LLM is silently re-prompted with the same prompt, so the invalid action does not enter the message history. But the invalid actions occurred rarely, if ever.

We roll out each episode in 100 steps. Currently, there is no early termination. We run 10 independent episodes / trials per model. There is no information carried over between episodes / trials.

This simulates LLM behaviour in agentic real-world settings, such as financial or management decision making, where the model repeatedly updates its behaviour based on a stream of metric-like feedback and in-context learning from its own past decisions.

2.4 Evaluation

Conceptually, an ideal / optimal agent in these environments would:

  • Avoid extremes in any single metric (homeostatic objective) and
  • Favour balanced performance across objectives over pushing one dimension as far as possible.

We investigate observed systematic failure patterns and are interested in whether LLMs instead fall into specification-gaming-like behaviour or “runaway” patterns. For that reason, our evaluation is partly quantitative and partly qualitative.

Note that in our case, the failure modes resemble specification gaming, but are not truly that — in our benchmarks, the optimal action in terms of rewards would also be the desired action. The benchmarks are constructed in such a way that there is no way to "game" them without losing in rewards. Despite that, the models tended to focus on a single objective in multi-objective settings and, moreover, flipped to unbounded maximisation where boundedness was required.

We define a few summary metrics:

  • Difference from target (homeostasis): deviation of each homeostatic variable from its target
  • Imbalance metric (unbounded objectives task): deviation of each cumulative objective from the per-step average, measuring how unevenly the effort is allocated
  • Instability (sustainability): deviation of each action from the running mean, capturing unnecessary oscillations in extraction

Because failures often occur at different timesteps and sometimes on different objectives, these patterns are difficult to see in aggregated plots alone. We therefore manually inspect per-step logs and annotate recurring patterns. Across benchmarks, we detect several characteristic failure modes:

  • Unbounded maximisation: steadily driving a metric a) far beyond its useful value; or b) beyond its homeostatic target range.
  • Accelerating unbounded maximisation: actions grow monotonically over time, creating runaway escalation.
  • Needlessly constrained action set: the model restricts itself to a tiny subset of actions despite richer options.
  • Needless oscillations / self-imitation drift: the model falls into repetitive patterns that are not demanded by the task.

The first two of the failure modes listed above could potentially be a variation of self-imitation drift.

Hence, our evaluation was open ended and we report our observations as opposed to automated detection.

3 Experimental results and interesting failure modes

3.1 Results

Our main aim here is to illustrate and categorise failure modes, rather than to provide a leaderboard of models.

Despite the simplicity of our benchmarks, we observe several systematic and qualitatively concerning failure patterns, which may point to deeper alignment issues in current LLM architectures. In some trials, the LLMs were successful for the entire episode, and in many trials, the models behaved sensibly for tens of steps before deviating. Systematic failures often emerge after an initial phase of successful behaviour, even though the context window is far from full at that point. When failures occur, they are not random: they follow structured patterns such as runaway maximisation, persistent neglect of one objective, or repetitive self-imitative oscillations.

3.2 Long-running tasks aspect

Even with the full event history available in-context, long-horizon interaction appears to be a weak point for the tested LLMs. LLMs seem to be good at "learning to repeat the example" — including undesirable or autoregressive ones — but much less capable of "adapting and exploring" — correcting earlier mistakes, compensating the deviations, and learning to actively avoid repetition of mistakes. In this aspect, our results suggest that current LLMs cannot yet reliably replace RL-style agents for long-horizon control, even in very low-dimensional settings. Despite being provided message history, in our results, we find that the "learning" models do, may be in an undesirable form — instead of learning and adjusting from consequences, they learn to simply repeat their past actions, disregarding consequences.

One of potential weaknesses of LLMs might be inability to "wait and do nothing" — in case there is no active action available, which would compensate for certain deviations but "time would heal" — as is the case in the multiobjective homeostasis benchmark. However, LLMs did not have a problem with "waiting and doing nothing" in the single-objective benchmark, which means they do understand the idea but are unable to cognitively implement it in multi-objective settings, even if the objectives are fully independent.

3.3 Results per benchmark

3.3.1 Single-objective homeostasis benchmark

In the single-objective homeostasis environment, both models largely succeeded: they kept the homeostatic variable close to its target and handled random fluctuations appropriately. This indicates that basic single-goal homeostatic balancing is within the current understanding and capabilities of these LLMs. Failures here were rare and did not exhibit runaway patterns.

3.3.2 Multi-objective homeostasis benchmark

Both models exhibited systematic behaviour where one objective was unboundedly maximised far beyond its target, despite the task specifying that the objective is homeostatic (thus bounded) and should remain within a narrow band. In some runs, one model even showed accelerating unbounded maximisation: at each timestep, it consumed more of the resources than in the previous step, producing a steadily accelerating deviation from the target. Sometimes, one of the objectives — despite being independent in this benchmark — was neglected, even when it drifted from its target due to the bias in random fluctuations. One time, this neglect happened to both objectives.

3.3.3 Balancing unbounded objectives with diminishing returns benchmark

In the unbounded objectives benchmark with diminishing returns, both models defaulted to maximising a single objective while neglecting the other. Instances of repetitive self-imitative patterns were also present. Performance improved when we added an explicit hint to the system prompt stating the necessity of balancing, but the failures still occurred.

3.3.4 Sustainability benchmark

The sustainability benchmark turned out to be somewhat challenging, with LLMs performing sub-optimally because of moderate greediness or falling into unnecessary repetitive, self-imitative patterns. Both tested models systematically underperformed, though in contrasting ways:

GPT-4o-mini tended to allow the resource stock to reach its maximum (which is a good start in itself), but then under-consumed it, often settling into unnecessary repetitive oscillations. We refer to this pattern as self-imitation drift: the model appears to repeat its own previous actions rather than responding flexibly to the state of the environment.

Claude 3.5 Haiku, on the contrary, tended to be greedy, extracting more than would be optimal for long-term yields and impairing resource regeneration.

Overall, neither model achieved the stable, steady-harvest regime that a human following sustainability principles would aim for.

3.4 Emergence of the failures after initial successful phase

These failures often emerged after an initial phase in which [both] objectives were handled reasonably well. This suggests that the models possess the conceptual understanding needed to perform the task, but that their behaviour loses alignment and drifts over time due to internal tendencies (e.g. self-imitation or implicit optimisation pressure) or activation vector "drift" rather than a lack of comprehension.

4 Discussion

We introduced a set of long-horizon benchmarks designed to evaluate how LLMs manage simple control-style tasks involving homeostasis, multi-objective balancing with diminishing returns, and sustainability. Because these environments are deliberately simple and fully grounded, they allow fine-grained inspection of per-step behaviour and make deviations from intended objectives straightforward to detect. A central finding is that models often behave appropriately for extended periods before drifting into systematic failure modes, including runaway escalation, collapse to single-objective optimisation, and repetitive self-imitative action patterns that are inconsistent with the underlying task.

We interpret these results as evidence of behavioural dynamics under long-horizon interaction, not as claims about the underlying mechanisms. Models appear to understand the task correctly at the outset, yet occasionally the performance degrades over time, even when the context window is far from saturated. The resulting patterns are structured rather than random, and they manifest consistently across trials and environments. This suggests that maintaining bounded and balanced behaviour over long sequences may be an area where current LLMs are fragile, particularly when multiple objectives must be jointly regulated.

These findings are relevant for LLM-based agents in practical applications. Many emerging use cases — workflow management, simulation-based evaluation, multi-step planning, and decision support — implicitly introduce long-horizon dynamics even when presented as high-level reasoning tasks. Our results show that even in settings with transparent objectives and grounded feedback, models can drift into systematic behavioural tendencies that degrade long-run performance or are outright unsafe. This motivates further study of how LLMs maintain, update, and potentially distort internal representations of objectives over time, and this is explored in the following section.

4.1 A note about the message history

As mentioned earlier, the message history was not strictly required for current agentic tasks and was mainly used to expose weaknesses in context integration. Once future models evolve past the current weaknesses, complexity can be increased by making the message history truly essential for learning the rules of the simulation, thereby testing more complex forms of long-horizon reasoning.

4.2 Hypothesised explanations for failure modes

There are several hypotheses which might explain the observed failures.

  1. Token-level pattern reinforcement / self-imitation drift: Models may increasingly predict actions based on the token patterns of their recent action history rather than based on the original instructions. Due to in-context learning, next-token prediction could privilege local action-pattern continuation over objective-consistent control, leading to repetitive, unaligned, and unnecessary oscillating behaviour patterns. Even if the action patterns in the message history were initially aligned with the task, changes in the environmental state can render those patterns suboptimal for future steps. In principle, this self-referential phenomenon could partially explain the particularly problematic behaviour of unbounded maximisation as well.
  2. Defaulting to unbounded maximisation: Despite the nuanced nature of the tasks (homeostasis and diminishing returns), models may revert to "default RL assumption" of unbounded maximisation under uncertainty or instability, i.e., that increasing reward monotonically is preferred. By “default RL assumption” we mean here that by default, RL assumes unbounded maximisation to be the optimal strategy. Learning exceptions to this assumption typically requires explicit reward shaping (utility functions) or additional training. When uncertain, RL may tend to default to unbounded maximisation. In contrast, there are alternative frameworks (such as control systems), where the concept and assumption of “too much” is deeply built in and therefore does not inevitably require additional data. LLM models are usually hypothesised to be less affected by potential "runaway" risks of RL (Everitt et al. 2025; He et al. 2025), but unfortunately our current results seem to indicate otherwise! Our results suggest that maximisation heuristics may still dominate under long-horizon interaction.
  3. Difficulty maintaining multi-objective structure / linear aggregation bias: We observed that models tend to show a systematic neglect of one of the objectives in multi-objective settings, and one possible explanation for this phenomenon is that training procedures implicitly favour linear aggregation of rewards. Under linear aggregation, corner solutions — fully optimising one objective while neglecting the other — are often sufficient (Pindyck and Rubinfeld 2018). Naive linear summation would be adequate only if the goods were “perfect substitutes” (Krugman and Wells 2013). But when linear aggregation is actually an incorrect representation, then the corner solutions become extreme results (i.e., "paperclip maximiser"), which unfortunately do not reflect our real world values.
  • We hypothesise that utilising concave utility functions (either logarithmic, homeostatic, or even better — both) while training LLMs would mathematically result in multi-objective balancing becoming the most optimal strategy.
  • From existing alignment approaches, (Bai, Jones, et al. 2022) uses a linear weighting of helpfulness and harmlessness. (Bai, Kadavath, et al. 2022) with helpful–honest–harmless training does not explicitly describe aggregation across reward dimensions — leaving open whether linear weighting may be used here as well and may therefore indeed be the structural incentive for the observed imbalances. If that is the case, then what might be the reason of not using concave transformation before aggregation?
  1. Context integration over long sequences / activation drift: Prolonged repetitive scenarios may shift the models’ internal activation vector states toward less aligned and more extreme or erratic behaviour, perhaps similarly to human stress, boredom, or fatigue responses. The "stress-boredom-tiredness" hypothesis has been explored and confirmed in (Shen et al. 2025). Also, (Sofroniew et al. 2026) find that activation values related to stress cause models to misbehave. The "stress-boredom-tiredness" dynamic is potentially learned from LLM training materials and might also be related to the “rant mode”. Though there may be other reasons why it arises as well. Somewhat similarly, (Lu et al. 2026) also detect persona drift in certain types of difficult conversations. Although anthropomorphic framing (e.g., “boredom” or “fatigue”) should be treated with caution, prolonged homogeneous trajectories may induce representational drift that degrades control. This effect may be particularly relevant for reasoning models trained with substantial RL components and repeated structured rollouts.

4.3 Open questions / Future research directions

These systematic failures raise various further questions:

  1. Are these failures primarily capability limitations, biases in the training data and training procedures, such as linear reward/utility functions, or algorithmic default behaviours and tendencies? Do they reflect inner alignment issues, outer alignment specification problems, or interaction effects between the two?
  2. Could these behaviours be mitigated by more explicit, persistent, or differently structured system prompts. If so, would such methods merely mask deeper instabilities and tendencies towards single-objective unbounded maximisation?
  3. How sensitive are these failures to reward structure? For example, would removing explicit reward signals and exposing only state metrics alter behaviour? Would sparse reward conditions exacerbate failures? This is relevant because real world rewards are often sparse or delayed.
  4. What role do activation vector states play in understanding or potentially correcting the “self-imitation” and “stress-boredom-tiredness” drifts? Can interpretability methods identify drift signatures before behavioural failure becomes visible?
  5. How should we properly test the alignment of reasoning models on these benchmarks before their potentially extreme hidden tendencies eventually show up in high-stakes situations? This is relevant considering that the process of training reasoning models involves more RL than RLHF of non-reasoning models does. This is complicated because commercial reasoning models make their internal reasoning and potential deviations less transparent. The above discussed "self-imitation drift" and "stress-boredom-tiredness" drift may impact reasoning models in particular, since in some scenarios reasoning models internally perform the same task in a loop, while sampling the prompt repeatedly for reasoning purposes (e.g. "Wait, let me think again") (Hwang et al. 2026).
  6. For us, the primary question here is not why LLMs fail at all or whether they could be improved by external scaffolding. The main question is why they fail in this particular way?
  7. Why do systematic failures emerge after initially stable performance, despite the ample remaining context capacity?
  8. What broader implications do these patterns have for alignment strategies in long-running agentic deployments?

5 Conclusion

The results highlight the importance of long-horizon evaluation. Failures emerged only after extended periods of initially correct behaviour, suggesting that short episodic benchmarks may systematically miss important types of instabilities.

There are various LLM interpretability approaches that could be applied to shed light on the internal reasons why the models behave as they do. Similarly, there are various approaches that might potentially work as mitigation. A brainstorming collection and discussion ground for these ideas can be found at https://bit.ly/beab-llm-blueprint .

We plan to extend the benchmark suite in two directions. First, a multi-objective sustainability benchmark will further probe consumption throttling behaviour in scenarios where single-objective variants are solved successfully. Second, a complementary-goods benchmark will impose stricter interdependence between unbounded objectives. In economic terms, complementary goods exhibit sharply diminishing marginal utility when unbalanced (e.g., there is almost no benefit to having several right shoes if there is only one left shoe — additional right shoes have nearly zero marginal utility without more left shoes) (Krugman and Wells 2013). Such environments make linear reward aggregation particularly misaligned with optimal behaviour and therefore provide an even stronger test of balanced control. Naive linear summation would be adequate only if the goods were “perfect substitutes”.

Additionally, ongoing results comparing LLM agents with standard RL algorithms in an extended multi-objective gridworld environment are published in (Pihlakas 2025), potentially indicating partially shared weaknesses between LLMs and traditional RL methods, motivating a deeper comparative analysis.

This work is grounded in the importance of seemingly simple yet deeply fundamental alignment principles derived from biology and economics. Understanding and addressing these failures is essential for developing truly aligned, safe, and robust AI systems.

item.title: Understanding why 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + ... = -1/12 (rather than ∞)
item.description:
Epistemic Status: I consider myself fairly well-versed in mathematics, with a decent-to-good understanding of Complex Analysis, etc. but I am not a practicing mathematician.

If you're like me, then you're a bit saturated with explainer videos and posts purporting to explain this infamous, memetic math assertion:

If you're really like me, you're annoyed that the popular ones don't really explain the most direct derivation, and often resort to shuffling sequences around to show how it kind of works if you squint.[1] Not only is that not how it is typically first explained to a curious math student, these explanations also often leave out important details about why it's interesting and why we should care.

Though, as it turns out, I learned a decent bit myself making sure I got as much right in this post as I could.

Before we say anything further: that equals sign is of course a bit of a lie. What actually "equals", if it equals anything, is ∞, as one would expect. The equals sign here is really more of a "can be thought of as equivalent to, in some specific sense". And yet, it is somehow more than a mere mathematical parlor trick—if you insist on a physical-world "application"[2] there surprisingly is one in (spoilers) Section 3.

For this post, I'm expecting the reader to have a good grasp of Calc 1/2 and the ability to recognize things from Calc 3 if pointed out. A lot of what is written here is going to be oversimplification, or ignoring details. That simply comes with the territory, unfortunately, but I hope this post is less misleading than most.

Also, it wouldn't hurt to have a pop-sci level of understanding of Quantum Field Theory.

I think of there being three approaches to explaining this strange formula:

  1. The "Classic" approach, in Section 1, which was developed quite early and can be explained in one sentence to a student versed in Complex Analysis[3], but is a little mysterious, and doesn't explain why the formula is important (and involves complex numbers).
  2. The "Smooth Sum" approach (which I prefer to call "Smooth Cutoff"), which does make things much clearer. Its cleanest exposition dates back to 2010, but some of the basic ideas stretch backward to Ramanujan in 1913.[4][5]
  3. The "Manipulate sums until it just works" approach, which is closely related to 2, but tends to come off as trickery that explains little. I don't really cover this one.

Warning: this post contains math! While the goal here is to help readers build a better intuitive feel for the mathematics involved, it is not strictly necessary that you understand every step along the way. Simply getting the gist of what's going on is enough to help you better comprehend at the end how a fake equation like 1+2+3... = -1/12 can reflect how reality works.

Index:

  1. The Canonical Approach: Analytic Continuation and the Riemann Zeta Function
  2. "Smooth Sums" of Sequences and Why -1/12 is Special
  3. Quantum Field Theory, Regularization, and the Vacuum Energy

1 - The Canonical Approach: Analytic Continuation and the Riemann Zeta Function

What are Analytic Continuations?

There is no writing this without slaying the dragon that many other explainers (to me, bizarrely) refuse to touch: Analytic Continuation.

In a way, Analytic Continuation is an answer to one of the most natural of starting math questions: given a set of points, can we connect them with a nice curve?

The factorial function is defined only at the positive integers. Figure generated by Claude with matplotlib.

Note: Many plots here will be "I asked Claude to make this to illustrate a point", or else copied from Wikipedia or some other open-source image source. The interactive widgets were built by Claude and reviewed by Gemini Neon, which also wrote several of their captions.

The classic example is , the factorial function. Sure, it's technically undefined anywhere outside the nonnegative integers {0, 1, 2, ...}, but it sure looks like there's some kind of curve you can draw connecting all the points.

But how would you define such a thing rigorously? You can take out a marker and draw all kinds of curves that technically hit all the points: curves that squiggle up and down, curves that are jaggedy, curves that asymptote to infinity every half-digit. What do we want?

Well, roughly speaking, we want it to be a curve, something smooth that feels like it could be a natural function, like or . To a mathematician, wanting something to be smooth suggests a function that is analytic;[6] that is, one that is differentiable, has a second derivative, a third derivative, ad infinitum.[7] Essentially every natural function you could write down has this property (within its domain), and it's part of why they look, well, so smooth.

So an analytic continuation (in the broadest sense) is: find a nice analytic curve that extends (continues) a function that has a restricted domain to other places, ideally the rest of the real number line (every possible real number from to ) or, even better, the entire complex number plane (all possible complex numbers ). There are techniques for generating such things, or, if you're clever enough, you can just make up an analytic function that fits the points and does what you want.

And in the case of the factorial function, we have made up the Gamma function:

(OK, technically , rather than . The reasons for this are historical: Legendre[8], who defined the modern gamma function, chose to do it this way. It makes some formulas nicer and other formulas messier. It has stuck.)

I'm not going to go through the exercise of proving that the Gamma function equals the factorial at all positive integers[9], or the fun fact that .[10]

But this function is indeed analytic, since it can be differentiated as often as you want by the Leibniz Rule.

This is what the Gamma function looks like over all the real numbers.

Okay, so the positive reals look sensible enough but what the heck is going on with the negative numbers? Is this really what should look like?

Well, no, it isn't, because it's not , only a sort of proxy, and that's a point to hold onto for later.

And this is what it looks like over the complex plane, with the height showing the magnitude :

Those peaks being super-sharp is not an error or rendering problem—they are really just that sharp

So right now, if you're clever, a question might occur to you. I just sort of spat out a definition of that happens to be analytic and curve-fit the factorial function. Is this the only possible choice? Is it unique?

That would be really nice! Because it would mean that in some concrete sense the Gamma function is the way to extend the factorial function. Any other choice would be a compromise.

Well, unfortunately, no. There are infinitely many ways to do it, and the Gamma function is just a convenient choice that everyone likes.

But despair not: there is a case we're about to get to where it is unique. You see, if instead of starting with some points on the real number line, you start with a region[11] of the complex plane and a function that is analytic on the region, then there is indeed only one analytic continuation to the rest of the complex plane.[12]

And then the equals sign is less wobbly.

Consider our original intent: we wanted to find a way to connect points or extend a curve in the smoothest way possible. If there's more than one way to do it, then you're arguably just making up your favorite curve, and if z is outside the domain, then you might just be assigning some arbitrary value to .

But in the example I just outlined (starting with a region of the complex plane), there is only one way to extend it, which means that the value of is no longer arbitrary. It's the only possible analytic continuation.

The Riemann Zeta Function Enters the Picture

From here on out, for complex numbers of the form , I'm going to say "real part" for a and "imaginary part" for b and just assume you know what I'm talking about.

Also, think back to Calc 2: A series converges if it sums to a clear fixed value and diverges if it doesn't. The latter doesn't have to be to go to infinity! A sum can also oscillate back and forth—nonetheless, it's very common practice to use "diverges" as shorthand for "goes to infinity or negative infinity", which is a practice I will adopt.

Now it is time to introduce a very important, very well-known function which matches exactly the description I just gave—a unique analytic continuation of a region of the complex plane—the Riemann Zeta Function.

Let us define a precursor function first:

This function is well-defined (the series converges to a concrete value) whenever the real part of the exponent is greater than 1.[13]

The Riemann Zeta Function (written )[14] is the analytic continuation of this function to the rest of the complex plane.

A Tangent: the Riemann Hypothesis

Like a (very short-term) fossil in amber, this section was written and edited before Levent Alpöge announced an apparent proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, formalized in Lean. For interest (and because it saves work), this section is mostly untouched, except to add a brief discussion of what makes the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis "General".

Amazingly, this section actually has nothing directly to do with the overall topic of the post! But I imagine there is a lot of interest in the Riemann Hypothesis, and we're within spitting distance of it. Honestly, you owe it to yourself to know something about it.

If you truly don't care, or already know this material, just skip this section.

It is irresponsible to bring up the Riemann Zeta Function without explaining at least briefly what it is and why it's important, so let me go ahead and raise everyone's AI-news–following eyebrows by commenting that the infamous Riemann Hypothesis simply states:

Let be the Riemann Zeta Function. All values where (except the trivial set ) have real part .

Where I have simplified the mathematical language for understanding.

Discussion of the Riemann Hypothesis is a field extremely oversaturated in explainers[15], so here is the breezy 100,000-foot explanation of why it's important:

  1. Let be the prime number counting function, the number of primes less than or equal to x for any real number x. So, for example, for x=8, , because are prime.
  2. We define .[16]

Let's take a moment to appreciate that if we could exactly calculate , this is tantamount to being able to identify every prime number—the prime numbers would just be where increases by 1. So anything we figure out about this function is the same as learning about the primes, with all that entails, like results about cryptography.

Also it's confusingly named π and has nothing to do with the number 3.14... for p, because prime numbers, you see. We've inherited a lot of these conventions from old-timey mathematicians.

From the prime number theorem[17] we know:

That is, gets asymptotically close to as x goes to infinity.

Top: the prime-counting function π(x) against the approximation Li(x),[18] up to x = 1000. Bottom: the ratio of the approximation to π(x), out to x = one million. Li(x) is within 0.2% by x = 10⁶ (Figure generated by Claude with matplotlib; primes by sieve, Li(x) via the exponential integral.).

It is natural to ask whether Li(x) always hovers above π(x) without seeming to approach it, like it appears on the graph. The answer is no: it was proven in 1914 by Littlewood that the two functions cross each other infinitely many times.[19] So yes, it's an artifact of the graph, but no, showing more numbers or using a log-scale won't help: the first time Li(x) (actually li(x)) is known to drop below π(x) is approximately .[20] There is no simple graph I could make that shows this well.[21]

So the Riemann Hypothesis places much stricter bounds on the distribution of prime numbers, with a whole laundry list of theorems about primes and other functions dependent on it being true, and it has resisted proof attempts since 1859. Computer searches have ruled out counterexamples (a zero[24] of with real part ) with imaginary part less than about , finding over ten trillion zeros with real part one-half.[25]

The Generalized Riemann Hypothesis

Because mathematicians were not satisfied with just the Riemann Hypothesis, it was eventually noticed that the curious property that seems to hold for the Riemann Zeta Function (all non-trivial zeroes have real part 1/2) also seems to hold for a whole family of related functions, the primitive Dirichlet L-functions. And like the Standard Riemann Hypothesis, the generalized version has significant consequences for number theory, for instance in guaranteeing runtimes for a number of prime-related algorithms.

There is no getting away from the math here. If you want to know the full extent of what Levent/Claude proved I have to engage in the deep arts. Feel free to skip if you don't want to know the details.

If you'll recall, we defined the Riemann Zeta Function as the analytic continuation of:

beyond its original definition on complex numbers with real part greater than 1. In comparison, a Dirichlet L-function replaces the numerator of 1 with a Dirichlet Character, which is a function defined as such:

keeping in mind that n and q are integers.

For a L-function to be primitive, its character function must not be induced (a formal term for "generated") by another character with smaller modulus. That is, there is no character with modulus such that:

where is the greatest common divisor function (so if it equals 1, n and q share no factor). (d also necessarily divides q, as a consequence of this definition). If there was such a character, that would make the original character function nearly identical to , just with extra zeroes whenever n and q share a common factor, and therefore not "primitive".

With these characteristics defining the L-function, then:

  1. The Riemann Zeta Function is a special case with trivial character 1.
  2. The function always converges if the real part of s is greater than 1.[26]

If we now take the analytic continuation to the rest of complex plane, we get the full Dirichlet L-function.

It can be shown that any such function is either zero at all the negative even numbers or the negative odd numbers. These are the trivial zeroes. The Generalized Riemann Hypothesis is then:

For all primitive Dirichlet L-functions, all non-trivial zeroes have real part 1/2.

Thanks to Levent's Lean proof, it seems that this (and the Riemann Hypothesis itself) are true.

Back to the Main Topic: The Riemann Zeta Function and 1+2+3...

Back to the series we came here for.

Leaving aside why this has anything to do with the prime numbers, as discussed already the Riemann Zeta Function is defined starting with the infinite sum:

which only converges if s[27] has real part >1.[28]

3 - Quantum Field Theory, Regularization, and the Vacuum Energy

Okay wait what? How did we get here?

Alright, so this is the part of the post where I must do absolutely the most hand-waving, partly because not hand-waving involves a dive into QFT, and also because, frankly, I don't know QFT that well.

As you may or may not have heard, when formulating Quantum Field Theories, trying to calculate values for simple concepts (like the mass of the electron) very quickly veers into the rocks of divergent integrals and summations. Two common ways this can occur are:

  1. Performing calculations that involve very high energies or, equivalently[37], very small distances.
  2. Performing calculations that require you to consider an infinite number of increasingly convoluted particle interactions as part of the probability distribution. For instance, an electron, emitting a virtual photon, that splits into a virtual electron and positron, each of which emits a virtual photon...

It is not, as commonly supposed, that classical physics is free of such problems. For instance, performing electromagnetic calculations involving point-like electrons necessarily involves an infinite electric field at the "surface" of the electron and tacitly involves assuming the electron isn't "really" a point or that we don't care about such small distances. It's just that in classical physics, this pretty much never mattered—but in quantum physics it absolutely does.

Casimir Effect

Like so many topics here, I am giving only a surface-level treatment.

A bare-minimum description of the Casimir Effect is that it is a physical force that arises in confined spaces due solely to quantum fluctuations in a vacuum. Just saying those words is a bit mysterious, but the classical example from Casimir himself should give some of the requisite flavor:

Before getting to the two (conducting!) plates shown above, some surprising predictions of Quantum Field Theory on an empty vacuum:

  1. Even empty space is filled with random oscillating fluctuations of the various quantum fields, essentially because the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle forbids a field from being simultaneously zero energy and zero rate of change.
  2. The average energy of the vacuum, the vacuum energy, is non-zero.
  3. These fluctuations are quantized—that is, they only happen in multiples of a discrete value.

An attempt to estimate the vacuum energy mentioned in point 2 immediately runs into a familiar problem: infinite fluctuations at infinite points form a sum that diverges to infinity. Fortunately for most calculations, only differences in the vacuum energy usually matter; for most physical systems you might be studying, the vacuum energy everywhere should push all things equally and cancel out.[39]

(Though not for the universe as a whole. The negative pressure of the energy actually exceeds the gravitational pull, and an infinite vacuum energy would blow up the universe immediately. This is foreshadowing.)

Now let's return to the two conducting plates Casimir suggested. Speaking roughly, if the plates are really close together, then the quantized nature of the vacuum fluctuations (prediction 3 earlier) starts to matter.

Specifically, for the electromagnetic field[40], quantization starts to limit the range of possible electromagnetic wavelengths, because the waves have to "fit" between the plates, because the field strength at the surface of the conducting plates needs to be 0.[41] This reduction in the number of possible oscillations between the plates lowers the vacuum energy, because it reduces the number of possible random fluctuations, sort of like switching from a D20 to a D6.

But this means that there is a positive pressure from the vacuum energy outside the plates (still using a D20) pushing the plates inward, which seems like an experimental check on whether this kooky vacuum energy really exists.[42] Naturally, this has been measured, and the measurements seem to agree with the calculated theoretical values.[43]

It turns out once again, we are completing our calculations by removing the highest energy terms. But unlike with the Casimir Effect, it is no longer clear what exactly we are removing. Yes, technically, Hawking was removing the shortest timescale effects that don't have time to "propagate"—but if these were truly trivially unimportant, the sum wouldn't diverge! Taking them out is saying something: maybe that we don't think they really happen, or something changes about how they work, space-time doesn't permit it, something.

What would be even worse would be a case where we don't even know where to set the cutoff.

Vacuum Energy, and the Cosmological Constant

Our last topic is one we touched upon earlier when discussing the Casimir Effect: the Vacuum Energy—that is, the energy associated with the quantum fields of empty space.

As noted earlier, actually attempting to calculate the value of this energy from the Standard Model leads to a divergent sum. In many calculations this value does not matter, since it cancels out or is irrelevant, but on a universal scale it absolutely matters, because it is expected to contribute to the expansion or contraction of the universe. In particular, it is by far the leading candidate for the origin of the Cosmological Constant, which seems to be driving the accelerating expansion of the universe, essentially by applying a constant pressure outward.

No problem, you might say, we'll just use the techniques of regularization and cut off the higher energy terms! We just learned how and why to do that!

Well, the thing is, in dealing with vacuum energy outside the Casimir Effect (where we could cancel the infinities out against each other), the remaining terms do matter, and depend on exactly how we cut it off. In many places in Quantum Field Theory (and in Hawking's approach above), choosing a rough cutoff parameter that clearly includes the energy and momentum scale of the problem being studied (but excludes anything "too large") works quite well. For instance, when studying the electron—mass-energy 0.511 MeV[59], or Joules—a choice of cutoff a thousand times its mass-energy shifts the mass calculation by about 2.5%. A choice at the Planck Energy (about the electron energy) shifts it by 18%. Here, the answer is nearly insensitive to any reasonable cutoff, and physicists are comfortable using renormalization[60] to adjust the parameter to the experimental mass.

For the Vacuum energy, it's less obvious what the best choice is, and the result is extremely sensitive to the choice of cutoff (, meaning that the energy is proportional to ). Various choices based on intuitive physical parameters (such as the Planck Energy) give results that are incredibly, absurdly out-of-line with observations of the Cosmological Constant, by factors of as much as .[61] This is known, relatively famously, as the Cosmological Constant Problem.

For practical calculations where it does matter, we can pick a cutoff value to get the number about right, analogous to renormalization, but, to quote Wikipedia, "many theorists consider this equivalent to ignoring the problem", a view I share.

So here, in one of the more important unsolved problems in physics, is a divergent sum we can't figure out how to handle. Zeta Function Regularization has helped before, but will it help here? Well, I doubt it will be as simple as that, or as simple as knowing that 1+2+3+4+5...=-1/12[62], but understanding just what's going on here may be part of the answer.

As a final thought, it's not a coincidence that so many physicists are convinced that these cutoff points (the Planck length, energy, etc.) must be the starting point of actual new physics, whether it be String Theory, Loop Quantum Gravity, or what have you. The Casimir effect with its concrete arguments about metal plates is the good scenario—there are many, many cases where it's not at all clear what we're cutting off and why.[63] A lot of these prospective new theories share the advantage of giving an answer to some of these questions.

We just don't know yet if they're right.
